change.hint: Three angles decide: how steeply the rails rise, how far they spread and how pointed the cone is.
change.spread_hint: Each rail's angle to the centre line, seen from above.
change.cone_hint: The angle between the cone's surface and its axis: the larger, the faster it thins towards its tips.
change.start_gap: Gap between the rails at the bottom
change.start_gap_hint: How far apart the rails are at the low end.

model.intro: The cone does what every body does: it rolls to where its centre of mass is lower. The only question is where that is.
model.thin: The double cone is thickest in the middle and thins evenly towards its tips.
model.rails: The rails spread as they go up, and rise.
model.axis: Where the rails are further apart, they hold the cone further out, where it is thinner: it sits lower between them. So the height of its axis is the rails' height plus a radius that shrinks towards the top.
model.condition: Both parts change evenly: the axis runs on a straight line. If it falls while the rails rise, the cone rolls up – exactly when tan γ is smaller than tan α · tan β.

symbols.r: the cone's radius at a distance y from its middle
symbols.y: the distance from the middle, along the axis
symbols.alpha: the cone angle, between surface and axis
symbols.x: the place along the rails, from the low end
symbols.d: each rail's distance from the centre line
symbols.z: the height of the cone's axis
symbols.c: the exact contact's factor, close to 1

sweet.heights: Over their whole length the rails rise by {{rise}} cm. The cone's axis {{direction}} by {{fall}} cm meanwhile.
sweet.threshold: Up to a slope of {{threshold}}° this cone rolls up; the rails here rise at {{slope}}°.
sweet.exact: Computed exactly, a rail that runs skew and rises touches the cone a little off the point under its axis. The engine finds that point: for the default exhibit the axis stands 1.002 times as high above the rail as the textbook assumes. At the boundary, though, the contact lies right under the axis – there the textbook's condition is exact.

figures.time: To the end of the rails

computed.energy: A single coordinate, the place along the rails. The cone rolls without slipping, so it spins as fast as its axis moves on, divided by the radius it is rolling on – which shrinks towards the top. The energy of motion, spin and height stays the same. Lagrange's method makes a second-order equation of it, which the engine solves with the Runge–Kutta method in steps of a millisecond.
computed.m: the slope of the axis's path
computed.rho: the radius the cone rolls on

at.vessel: A round vessel of water stands on a turntable. As it turns, the water sinks in the middle and climbs the wall, the more the faster it turns.
at.dry: For the default vessel – 30 cm across, filled 10 cm deep – the middle runs dry at 126 turns a minute.

parabola.refused: The water has to stand in the vessel: the depth of filling must be less than the vessel is high.

play.title: Turn the turntable
play.hint: Set the speed. The vessel follows at once, the water takes its time – in fast motion you see it catch up.
play.spills: This fast the water climbs over the rim: it spills.

views.side: The vessel cut through: the water under its hollowed surface, dashed its level at rest, and the focus of the bowl as a mirror
views.top: The vessel from above: marks on the rim turn with the vessel, specks in the water with the water
views.top_caption_turning: From above, turning with the vessel: the specks show how far the water still lags

change.title: Change the exhibit
change.hint: A wider vessel or less water runs dry sooner; a shallow one spills sooner.

model.intro: When the water turns with the vessel as one body, its surface everywhere stands square to gravity and the centrifugal pull together. The centrifugal pull grows with the distance from the axis, so the surface grows steeper outwards.
model.surface: That makes a paraboloid: the height grows with the square of the distance from the axis.
model.volume: The water stays the same. So the middle sinks by exactly as much as the rim rises: by ω²R²/(4g).
model.dry: From this speed on the middle touches the bottom. Faster, a dry patch opens there and grows with the speed.

symbols.z: the surface's height above the bottom
symbols.omega: the angular velocity: 2π times the turns a second
symbols.dry: the angular velocity at which the middle runs dry
symbols.f: the focal length of the bowl as a mirror

sweet.equal: At {{rpm}} turns a minute the middle sinks by {{drop}} cm – and the rim rises by exactly as much. The two lines part symmetrically until the middle reaches the bottom.
sweet.dry: The middle is dry: from {{rpm}} turns a minute the water stands in a ring only.
sweet.mirror: A turning bowl of a liquid that reflects is a telescope's mirror: light coming straight down meets at the focus. The speed sets the focal length – one turn in 8.5 s puts it 9 m up.
sweet.spin_up: Switch the turntable on from rest to this speed, and the water takes about {{tau}} s to reach two thirds of it:

computed.system: How long the water takes to follow the vessel: the bottom drags it along through a thin boundary layer (after Greenspan and Howard, one Ekman layer at the bottom). The page lets the water's speed follow the vessel's over this time, about half a minute for the default vessel, and draws the surface as if the water turned as one body. That is a model of how long it takes, not of the flow meanwhile.
computed.big_omega: the larger of the two angular velocities

at.pair: Two equal pendulums hang side by side, joined below their pivots by a soft spring. One is pulled aside and let go; the other hangs still.
at.wanders: Soon the second starts to swing while the first comes to rest – then the other way round, again and again. For the default pair the swing wanders over and back once in 23 s.

coupled.refused: The spring has to sit between the pivot and the bob on both pendulums: the right one is too short for the spring this low.
coupled.view: The two pendulums from the front, the spring between them

play.title: Push the pendulums
play.hint: Choose how the pendulums are let go. The bars show how much of the energy is in each right now.

change.title: Change the exhibit
change.hint: A stiffer spring, or one fixed lower, couples more strongly: the swing wanders faster. Unequal lengths let only part of it over.
change.spring_hint: How hard the spring pulls when stretched by a metre.
change.spring_at_hint: How far below the pivots the spring is fixed.
change.right_length_hint: The left one is 50 cm long.

model.intro: Each pendulum swings under gravity, and the spring pulls it towards the other, as hard as the two have moved apart at its height.
model.equation: The left pendulum's equation; the right one's is built alike, with the spring pulling the other way.
model.modes: Two motions in which both swing at one beat: together, the spring idle, as fast as one pendulum alone; and against each other, the spring working too, faster. Every other motion is a sum of these two.
model.beat: Push only one pendulum and that is half of each. The two drift slowly apart and together again: the swing wanders over and back once in this time.

symbols.a: how far below the pivots the spring is fixed
symbols.omega: the angular frequencies together and against each other
symbols.beat: the time the swing takes to wander over and back
symbols.kappa_i: the coupling as each of the two pendulums feels it

sweet.modes: What nature swings here is not one pendulum and then the other, but the two shared beats. The wandering swing is their sum – which is why it does not wander for “Both alike” and “Against each other”.
sweet.beat: Here the swing wanders over and back once in {{beat}} s, and {{share}} % of it reaches the other pendulum.
sweet.unequal: Unequal pendulums never hand over all of it: only this share, the more the more alike the pendulums and the stronger the spring.

computed.system: Four first-order equations, the swings and their speeds, with the full sine and the spring between them. The engine solves them together with the Runge–Kutta method a millisecond at a time; the page does the same with the same steps, a few dozen a frame.

at.peg: A pendulum swings in front of a wall. Below its pivot sits a peg: each time the string swings through the vertical, the peg catches it, and the bob swings on round a smaller circle about the peg.
at.height: The path is different, the height is not: the bob rises exactly to the line it was let go from. Set the peg low enough and it cannot – it swings right over, or the string goes slack.

peg.refused: The peg has to sit between the pivot and the bob.
peg.view: The pendulum, the peg and, dashed, the height the bob was let go from; the peg can be moved with a finger

play.title: Let the pendulum go
play.hint: Drag the peg up or down, or pick one of the three cases below.
play.outcome_same_height: At the peg the bob rises exactly as high as on the other side.
play.outcome_slack: Too much swing for the small circle, too little to go over: the string goes slack.
play.outcome_over_the_top: Swing enough: the bob goes right over the peg.

events.released: The string comes off the peg.
events.slack: The string goes slack: the bob flies free.
events.over_the_top: Over the top: the string winds round the peg.

change.title: Change the exhibit
change.hint: Every change lets the bob go again.
change.peg_hint: How far below the pivot the peg sits.

model.intro: The string always pulls across the bob's motion. It turns the bob, but does no work: whatever motion the bob has, it has from its fall alone.
model.energy: So its speed depends only on how far it is below the height it was let go from – whichever circle it is on. At the top, where it turns, it is back at that height.
model.pull: A string can only pull. Above the peg it has to hold the bob on its circle, and gravity helps; is the bob too slow there, the string would have to push – it goes slack, and the bob flies free until the string is taut again.

symbols.z: its height above the lowest point
symbols.h: the height it was let go from
symbols.r: the small circle's radius: the string's length less the peg's depth
symbols.phi: the angle round the peg, from below
symbols.z_slack: the height at which the string goes slack

sweet.height: The path changes, the height does not: the energy remembers where the bob came from. That is how Galileo showed that a ball rolling down a ramp rises as high again on any ramp opposite.
sweet.loop: It goes over the peg when let go from at least two and a half radii of the small circle: at the top it must still be fast enough for the string to pull.
sweet.slack: In between, the string goes slack at this height.
sweet.now: Here the bob was let go {{h}} cm above the lowest point; going over would take {{loop}} cm.

computed.system: Three motions, an equation each: the pendulum round the pivot, the shorter one round the peg, and free flight while the string is slack. The engine steps on with the Runge–Kutta method a millisecond at a time and finds each switch – the peg catching, the string coming off, going slack, jerking taut – within its step by halving, so that it happens exactly where it belongs.
computed.gravity: gravity, which alone acts in free flight

at.wheel: A heavy wheel sits on a thin axle, and two strings hanging from above are wound round the axle. The wheel is turned up until the strings are wound on, and let go.
at.climbs: It rolls slowly down, turns round at the bottom with a jerk and winds itself back up, nearly to where it was let go. The default wheel falls in 3.3 s and climbs to 94 % of the height before each time.

maxwell.refused: The axle has to be thinner than the wheel.
maxwell.view: Maxwell's wheel from the front on its two strings

play.title: Let the wheel go
play.hint: In the slowest motion you see the jerk at the bottom: the strings stretch by a few millimetres and throw the wheel back.

phases.jerk: At the bottom: the strings stretch and throw it back.
phases.up: It is winding itself back up.

change.title: Change the exhibit
change.hint: A thinner axle, or a wheel heavier at its rim, falls more slowly – and makes the jerk at the bottom harder.
change.loss_hint: The strings bend round the axle and rub: this share of their pull as a braking torque.
change.stiffness_hint: How hard both strings together would pull if stretched by a metre. Stiffer: a shorter, harder jerk.

model.intro: The strings come off the axle without slipping: for every centimetre the wheel falls, it turns on by a centimetre of the axle's circumference. Because the axle is thin, that means a great deal of spin for little fall.
model.roll: The wheel falls uniformly accelerated, but with only a small part of gravity's acceleration: k says how much harder the wheel is to set spinning than to set moving.
model.tension: So while it rolls, the strings carry nearly the whole weight.
model.share: This share of the energy of motion is in the spin – 98.8 % for the default wheel.

symbols.a: the wheel's acceleration as it rolls down
symbols.i: the wheel's moment of inertia: ½·M·R² for a disc, M·R² for a ring
symbols.s: the stiffness of both strings together
symbols.v: the wheel's speed when the strings have run out

sweet.spin: Nearly all the energy is in the spin – {{share}} % here – which is why the wheel falls so slowly: what the height gives goes into turning, not into falling.
sweet.jerk: At the bottom the strings' stretch catches the fall. For {{ms}} ms their pull rises to {{peak}} N, {{times}} times the weight. The spin goes on through the jerk and winds the strings back on from the other side.
sweet.climbs: Each time the wheel climbs to {{share}} % of the height before: the strings' rubbing on the axle takes a little as they wind off and on.

computed.system: Everything here has a closed form; nothing needs stepping: falling and climbing are uniformly accelerated, and in the jerk the wheel makes half a spring's swing on the stretched strings. For every frame the page asks where the wheel is.
computed.z: how far the strings are stretched in the jerk

at.pendulum: A second pendulum hangs from the end of a first. Pushed gently, both swing calmly to and fro; pushed hard, the lower arm flails, goes over the top, stops short and flails on – never the same way twice.
at.twice: Whoever pushes it twice “the same” sees two different dances. Here that is done more precisely than by hand: two pendulums whose starts differ by a thousandth of a degree.

chaos.view: The double pendulum and its twin, started a tiny angle differently, with the trail of the lower weight

play.title: Let two pendulums go
play.hint: The strong pendulum and its paler twin start almost alike. Watch when they part.

change.title: Change the exhibit
change.hint: Every change lets both go again.

model.intro: Two masses on two light rods, the lower hung from the end of the upper. The equations of motion follow from the energy by Lagrange's method; they are long but hold no mystery – and they have no closed solution.
model.energy: The double pendulum's energy: the motion of both masses, their coupling through the angle between the arms, and their height. Without damping it stays the same – that is the computation's check.
model.modes: For small swings everything is orderly: two modes, slow together and fast against each other (here for equal arms and masses).
model.lyapunov: For large swings a tiny difference grows by the same factor every second until it is as large as the motion itself. The rate of that growth is the Lyapunov exponent.

symbols.theta: the two arms' angles from the vertical
symbols.omega: the angular frequencies of the two modes
symbols.d: the gap between the two pendulums, in angles and angular velocities

sweet.gap: The gap between the two pendulums over time, on a logarithmic scale: a straight line means it grows by the same factor every second.
sweet.chaotic: Measured for this start: λ = {{lambda}} a second. A difference thus doubles every {{doubling}} s. Making it a thousand times smaller buys only ten doublings' time – which is why the pendulum cannot be predicted, though every computation is exact.
sweet.regular: Measured for this start: λ = {{lambda}} a second, practically zero. Swung this gently the difference stays small: the pendulum is predictable.

computed.system: Four first-order equations, both angles and their speeds, with the Runge–Kutta method in steps of a millisecond, for the pendulum and its twin. The engine measures the exponent Benettin's way: a twin starts a hundred-millionth away, every tenth of a second the gap's growth is noted and the twin set back to the small gap. The mean of the logarithms is the exponent – whatever small gap is chosen.
computed.d0: the small gap the twin is set back to each time
computed.dk: the gap after the k-th tenth of a second

at.wheel: Cups with a hole in the bottom hang all round a wheel. Water pours in at the top and drips out below. Turn the tap on and the top cup grows heavy, the wheel tips away and starts to turn.
at.never: Now it turns one way for a long time, slows, stalls, and turns the other way – when, and how often, keeps no beat. It never repeats.

views.wheel: The waterwheel with its cups, the tap above
views.butterfly: The wheel's path through the space of its states: its rate against the height of the water's spread – Lorenz's butterfly

play.title: Turn the tap on
play.hint: The tap decides: too little water and the wheel stands still; more, and it turns steadily; more still, and it turns chaotic.
play.tap_hint: ρ: how much water flows in, measured against the leaks and the brake.
play.brake_hint: σ: how hard the axle brakes, measured against the wheel's inertia and the leaks.
play.regime_still: Too little water: the leaks carry it off before the top cup grows heavy enough. The wheel stands.
play.regime_steady: The wheel turns steadily one way – which way, the first small nudge decides.
play.regime_chaotic: Chaos: no steady turning holds. The wheel changes direction without ever following a pattern.

model.intro: What counts is how the water is spread round the wheel – more precisely, how far its centre of mass lies to the side of the axle and above or below it. With that and the wheel's rate three equations can be written.
model.wheel: The water's spread turns with the wheel, water flows in at the top and leaks out everywhere; gravity turns the wheel when the water lies to one side, and the axle brakes.
model.lorenz: With time in units of the leaks and suitably scaled they are exactly Lorenz's equations, which he drew from a model of the air's flow in 1963 – with b = 1 instead of 8/3.
model.hopf: Above this inflow even steady turning is no longer stable: the wheel turns chaotic.

symbols.ab: how the water is spread: to the side, and top against bottom
symbols.q: how much water flows in at the top
symbols.x: the rate in units of the leaks
symbols.yz: where the water's centre of mass lies, suitably scaled
symbols.sigma: the brake against inertia and leaks
symbols.rho: the inflow against brake and leaks

sweet.lorenz: The wheel's speed over 200 seconds. In 1963 Lorenz looked for a simple model of the weather and found these three equations – and that tiny differences at the start make the forecast worthless after a short while. The waterwheel is that model to touch.
sweet.chaotic: In 200 seconds the wheel here turns back {{reversals}} times, never to the same beat.
sweet.steady: At this inflow the wheel, once started, turns steadily at {{rpm}} turns a minute.
sweet.still: At this inflow the wheel stands still.

computed.system: Three first-order equations, Lorenz's, with the Runge–Kutta method in steps of a hundredth of the leaks' time. Turned back, they give the wheel's rate and how full each cup is. The test computes the wheel's own equations in seconds and finds the same numbers.
computed.tau: time in units of the leaks

at.swing: A heavy pendulum on a long cable swings calmly to and fro, for hours. Nothing pushes it sideways – and yet after an hour its plane of swing points another way.
at.pins: A ring of pins stands on the floor; one after another falls as the plane sweeps past it. In Winterthur it turns by 11.1° an hour, clockwise: right round in 32.5 hours.

foucault.view: The pendulum from above: its plane of swing dashed, the bob's trail and the ring of pins

play.title: Let the Earth turn
play.hint: In fast motion you see the plane wander and the pins fall. Choose another place and the pace changes.
play.latitude_hint: Positive in the north, negative in the south.
play.never: At the equator the plane does not turn.
play.full_turn: Turning right round takes {{hours}} hours here.

change.title: Change the exhibit
change.hint: Length and swing change the swing's beat, not how fast the plane turns.

model.intro: The floor turns with the Earth. Someone standing on it therefore sees the pendulum pushed aside by a force that appears only in the turning frame: the Coriolis force.
model.coriolis: The bob is pulled back to the middle and pushed across its motion by the Coriolis force – to the right in the north.
model.latitude: How fast the floor turns under the pendulum depends on the latitude: at the pole with the Earth's whole turn, at the equator not at all.

symbols.xy: where the bob is above the floor
symbols.omega_z: how fast the floor turns under the pendulum
symbols.omega: the Earth's turn, once a sidereal day

sweet.floor: The pendulum keeps its plane in space; the floor turns away beneath it. In Winterthur at {{rate}}° an hour: so Foucault showed in Paris in 1851 that the Earth turns, without looking at the sky.
sweet.period: One swing takes {{period}} s here; the plane turns regardless. A shorter pendulum shows the same, as long as it keeps swinging long enough.

computed.system: For small swings the equation is linear and has a closed solution: a swing whose plane turns with the floor. With it the page shows any hour at once, without stepping there; the test holds it to a stepped solution over a hundred swings.
computed.zeta: the bob's place as a complex number
computed.omega_p: the swing's angular frequency in the turning frame

at.seats: A round platform turns slowly; two people sit opposite each other at its edge and roll a ball across.
at.misses: The ball curves away and misses, though nobody pushes it. At 6 turns a minute a straight throw at 3 m/s misses the other seat by 86°; aiming 50° ahead hits it.

coriolis.view: The carousel from above: the two seats, the aim dashed and the ball's path

play.title: Aim and throw
play.hint: Throw straight at the other seat once, then switch to “From outside”: there the puck flies straight.
play.aim_hint: How far beside the other seat it is aimed, anticlockwise positive.
play.no_lead: At this speed no throw reaches the other seat: it turns away too fast.

model.intro: Seen from outside, there is no force pushing the puck aside. When it leaves the hand it has two velocities: the throw, and the speed at which the thrower is carried round at the edge.
model.puck: So seen from outside it flies straight – just not to where the thrower aimed.
model.riding: Whoever rides along sees the same path curved, and explains it with two forces that appear only in the turning frame: the Coriolis force across the motion and the centrifugal force outward.
model.ball: A rolling ball is stranger still: the platform keeps turning under it, and the friction that keeps it rolling turns its velocity steadily along – at 2/7 of the platform's rate. Seen from outside, it runs on a circle.

symbols.r0: where the ball is let go
symbols.u: the throw, measured on the carousel
symbols.primed: acceleration, velocity and place as a rider measures them
symbols.k: how hard the ball is to set spinning: 2/5 for a solid ball

sweet.nobody: Nobody pushes the ball aside. The curve comes from turning along oneself: while the ball is on its way, the other seat moves on. The same “force” on the turning Earth steers the winds into low-pressure areas and makes them circle there.
sweet.ball: And a rolled ball is not straight even from outside: rolling on the turning platform, it runs on a circle at 2/7 of the carousel's rate.

computed.system: Both paths have closed forms: the puck on a straight line, the ball on a circle, both seen from outside and turned back for the rider. Where the ball reaches the edge again, and where one must aim to hit, the page finds by halving. The test holds the puck's turned-back path to a stepped solution with the Coriolis and the centrifugal force.

at.row: Five steel balls hang on strings in a row, just touching. Lift the first and let it fall: at the other end the last one flies off, and the three between seem to stand still.
at.two: Let two fall and two fly off. After a while the balls in the middle begin to swing too.

cradle.view: Newton's cradle from the front: the beam, the strings and the balls

play.title: Lift and let go
play.hint: Let one ball fall, then two. With 0.1 mm of air between the balls the sum comes out exactly.
play.restitution_hint: The share of their speed at which two balls part after meeting at 1 m/s. 1 means: nothing lost.
play.far_hint: After the first collision: the share of the energy in as many balls at the other end as were lifted.
play.after: Speeds after the first collision, left to right: {{speeds}} m/s

chart.caption: Second by second, each ball's widest swing since it was let go

model.intro: Each ball is a pendulum. Two balls push on each other only where they dent each other a little – by Hertz's law, which grows stiffer the deeper the dent.
model.hertz: The force between two balls grows as the dent to the power 3/2; the second factor takes a little energy from the collision.
model.brief: Let a 64 g ball fall from 30° and its collision lasts about 0.2 milliseconds; for that moment the balls press on each other with nearly 900 N – as much as the weight of 90 kg.
model.swing: Each ball swings on its strings and is pushed by its neighbours.
model.why: When balls meet one at a time, momentum and energy are kept, and for equal balls that means: they trade speeds. Two balls at half the speed would have the same momentum but only half the energy.

symbols.delta: how far the two dent each other
symbols.k: the stiffness of two balls by Hertz
symbols.e_star: the steel's stiffness: Young's modulus E, Poisson's ratio ν
symbols.r_star: the effective radius of two equal balls of diameter d
symbols.alpha: the damping in the steel, set from e at 1 m/s
symbols.e: the share of the speed a collision gives back
symbols.theta: the angle of the i-th ball
symbols.l: the length from the hanging point to the middle of the ball
symbols.fi: the force between the i-th ball and its right-hand neighbour
symbols.v: the falling ball's speed at the bottom

sweet.wave: The balls touch, so they do not meet one after another: the collision runs through the row as a wave. Because Hertz's contact grows stiffer as it dents, the wave stays short and arrives almost whole in the last ball – 97 % of the energy. The others keep the rest; the first even bounces back a little.
sweet.gap: With 0.1 mm of air between the balls they meet one at a time again, and the sum comes out: 99.9 % of the energy in the last ball.
sweet.two: Let two fall and two waves run through the row one behind the other. The last ball flies off at 0.70 m/s, the one before it at 0.49 m/s – not both at the 0.63 m/s the two came in with. Together they still carry 97 % of the energy.
sweet.together: What stays in the row grows with every collision if the collisions lose a little energy: in the fourth second the middle ball already swings 2.5° wide. If every collision gives everything back (e = 1), it stays nearly still.

computed.system: Each ball is stepped by Runge–Kutta: a millisecond at a time while all swing free, a microsecond while two touch or are about to. The collision's figures come from the falling balls' first meeting with the hanging ones. When the balls press on each other for long, the page does not always keep up and runs a little slower for a moment. The test holds the largest force between two balls to Hertz's closed form, and checks that with air between the balls exactly one flies off, as fast as the first came in.

at.funnel: A wide funnel, almost flat at the edge and ever steeper towards the middle. A ball pushed off at the rim circles the hole in the middle for a long time.
at.faster: With every lap it circles lower and faster, at last in a whirl, until it drops in.

well.view_top: The funnel from above: contour lines every 2 cm, the hole, the ball and its track
well.view_side: The funnel cut through from the side, with the ball at its height

play.title: Push off and let it circle
play.hint: “Circle” pushes the ball off exactly as fast as keeps it on a circle without friction. With friction it sinks lap by lap; the chart holds every lap against Kepler.
play.aim_hint: Against the rim's direction, positive towards the hole.
play.resistance_hint: The share of the wall's push that brakes the ball. 0 means: no friction.
play.dropped: Dropped into the hole after {{t}} s and {{laps}} laps.
play.out: Rolled out over the rim: pushed too fast, or too steeply outward.

chart.caption: Every lap of the ball beside the lap time of a circle at that distance

model.intro: The ball rolls on the funnel's wall. As for a planet, what counts is how hard it is pulled towards the middle – here, by the wall's slope.
model.wall: The funnel's wall: the nearer the middle, the deeper, and its slope falls off outward as 1/r².
model.circle: On a circle the slope supplies the pull to the middle – as 1/r², like the Sun's gravity. The 5/7 comes from rolling: part of every push sets the ball spinning.
model.kepler: Kepler's third law follows: the square of the lap time grows as the cube of the distance.
model.resistance: Rolling resistance brakes the ball with a small part of the force with which the wall pushes on it.

symbols.z: the wall's height, measured from the height it nears far outward
symbols.n: the force with which the wall pushes on the ball

sweet.kepler: The lower, the faster – like Mercury against Neptune. At the start, twelve times as far from the middle as the hole's edge, a lap takes 5.1 s; at the hole only 0.12 s, 42 times less. That is Kepler's third law, and the funnel keeps it because its slope falls off outward as the Sun's gravity does: every lap of the ball meets the lap time of its circle to 3 %.
sweet.faster: Friction brakes the ball – and yet it gets faster. It loses energy, sinks to a lower circle, and there the circle's speed is higher. From the circle at the start it drops in after 46 s and 75 laps, 42 of them in the last 10 seconds, at last more than three times as fast as at the start. A satellite braked by thin air also sinks and speeds up.
sweet.rosette: Here the likeness ends. Without friction and not pushed exactly on a circle – at 0.30 m/s instead of 0.44 m/s – the path does not close into an ellipse as a planet's does: its point nearest the middle moves on by 40° every lap. The steep wall and its curvature have their say.

computed.system: The ball rolls without slipping; its spin counts as 2/5 more inertia, so every push along the wall moves it at 5/7. The equations of motion on the surface, in distance and angle, are solved by Runge–Kutta in steps of a millisecond. Rolling resistance acts against the wall's whole push, including the part that holds the ball on its curved path. The test checks energy and angular momentum without friction, the circle, and the time to the hole against an independent count from the circles' energy.
computed.left_out: Left out: the ball's spin about the wall's normal, its size beside the wall's curvature, air. A coin, which rolls on its edge and leans, is another problem.

at.rods: Six steel rods of different lengths stand clamped in a table that a motor shakes a little from side to side.
at.one: At one beat a single rod swings wide while the others stay almost still. A little faster, and another takes over.

resonance.view: The rods from the front on their table, each with its own frequency below it

play.title: Find the beat
play.hint: Shake the table and move the beat slowly. “Sweep” raises it by itself and records how far each rod swings meanwhile.
play.beat_hint: How many times a second the table goes to and fro.
play.sweeping: The beat rises by 0.05 Hz a second; move the slider to stop it.
play.damping_hint: How fast a rod comes to rest by itself: the share of the damping at which it would not swing at all.
play.sound_hint: Each rod sounds at its own frequency, seven octaves up, as loud as it swings.

chart.caption: How far each rod swings when the table keeps one beat long enough; dashed, what of it arrives during a sweep

model.intro: Each rod is clamped at the bottom and free at the top. Of its ways to vibrate only the first counts here: the whole rod bending to one side.
model.frequency: Its own frequency: the longer the rod, the lower – as the square of its length.
model.motion: The table shakes, and its acceleration pushes each rod, weighted by Γ = 1.566 for the first mode's shape. The damping takes swing away.
model.steady: Shaken at one beat long enough, the tip swings this far. In step (r = 1) that is Γ·Y/(2ζ).

symbols.beta: the first solution of cosh β · cos β = −1: 1.8751
symbols.i: the second moment of area of a round rod of diameter d
symbols.q: how far the tip swings against the table
symbols.omega: the rod's own frequency, as an angular frequency
symbols.zeta: the damping, as a share of the damping at which the rod would not swing at all
symbols.gamma: how hard the shaking pushes the first mode's shape
symbols.r: the table's beat divided by the rod's own frequency
symbols.y: how far the table goes to and fro

sweet.step: A small push at the right beat moves more than a big one at the wrong. The table goes only 1 mm to and fro; in step with the 80 cm rod, at 2.21 Hz, its tip swings 78 mm, its neighbours at most 4 mm. Three per cent off the beat, only 26 mm.
sweet.patience: Resonance needs patience: at 2.21 Hz the swing grows in 7.2 s to just under two thirds. Sweep faster and you miss it: at 0.05 Hz a second the same rod swings at most 40 mm, half as far, and only at 2.4 Hz.
sweet.everywhere: The same keeping in step shatters a glass at the right note, sets a bridge swinging under marching feet and lets a string take up an instrument's note.

computed.system: Each rod is computed as a single vibration: its first mode at its own frequency, pushed by the table's shaking, by Runge–Kutta in steps of a millisecond. During a sweep the beat rises between the steps. The test holds the first mode's constants to every table's values (β₁² = 3.516, Γ = 1.566) and the stepped solution to the closed form.
computed.sound: The sound is made in the browser and stays off until you turn it on; nothing of it is stored or sent.
computed.left_out: Left out: the higher modes (the second lies 6.27 times higher), the rod's stiffening at wide swings, the table's give.

at.wheel: A heavy wheel on an axle hangs on a string by one end of the axle. Let go still, it drops at once. Spinning fast, the axle stays nearly level and the wheel wanders slowly round the string.
at.suitcase: Next to it stands a suitcase in which such a wheel spins. Whoever carries it and turns a corner feels it tip sideways.

gyroscope.view: The wheel on its string, seen from a little above, one spoke coloured
gyroscope.trace: The axle's track: how far it sinks below its starting height, over the last turn round the string
gyroscope.trace_caption: The axle's track over the last turn round the string: how far it sinks below its starting height

play.title: Spin and let go
play.hint: Let the wheel go still once, then at 200 rpm. Shown four times slower, the axle can be seen nodding.
play.tilt_hint: From the upward vertical: 90° means level.
play.suitcase_hint: Whoever turns the suitcase with this wheel a quarter turn a second round a corner must supply this torque across it.
play.dropped: Without spin the wheel falls: after {{t}} s it hangs almost straight down.

model.intro: A spinning wheel has angular momentum along its axle. Gravity pulls on the wheel, the string holds the axle's end: that makes a torque across the axle, level.
model.torque: A torque changes the angular momentum in its own direction – and that is level, across the axle. So the axle turns sideways instead of falling.
model.precession: How fast the axle wanders round the string: the faster the wheel spins, the slower.
model.lagrange: What the page computes: the axle's tilt by Lagrange, for a top with one fixed point. The angular momentum about the axle and that about the string are kept meanwhile.
model.suitcase: Whoever turns the axle must supply this torque across it; without it the suitcase tips.

symbols.omega_p: how fast the axle wanders round the string
symbols.d: the distance from the string to the wheel's middle
symbols.i3: the moment of inertia about the axle: a hoop of radius r
symbols.omega3: how fast the wheel spins on its axle
symbols.theta: the axle's tilt from the vertical
symbols.phi: how far the axle has wandered round the string
symbols.i1: the moment of inertia across the axle, about its end
symbols.turn: how fast the suitcase is turned

sweet.sideways: The wheel does not give way in the direction it is pulled, but across it. Without spin it hangs almost straight down after 0.37 s; at 200 turns a minute the axle stays up and wanders once round the string in 8.1 s. Spun twice as fast, it wanders half as fast.
sweet.nod: It does not quite go without falling, though: let go, the axle first sinks by 3.2°, overshoots the steady wandering and comes back – it nods, a little over four times a second, and its track draws arches with points. As deep as energy and the two kept angular momenta allow, and no deeper.
sweet.suitcase: That is why the suitcase tips: turning it with this wheel a quarter turn a second round a corner takes 5.9 N·m across – as much as 600 g at the end of a metre rule.

computed.system: The wheel is a symmetric top with a fixed point, the axle's end on the string; its mass sits in the hoop. By Lagrange two angular momenta are kept, about the axle and about the string; only the tilt is stepped, by Runge–Kutta in steps of a millisecond. The test checks the energy, the steady wandering, and how deep the axle sinks against the count from the kept quantities alone.
computed.left_out: Left out: that the string itself swings and stretches (its end is the fixed point), friction in the bearing and at the string, air. Spokes and hub count for nothing beside the hoop.

at.stones: An arch is built of loose stones, without mortar. Once the last stone is set in the middle, the arch carries itself and a load besides.
at.chain: Next to it a chain hangs between two hooks. Turned upside down, its shape is the best shape for an arch.

arch.view: The arch from the front: the stones, the thrust line, the joints where it would open first, and the load

play.title: Build an arch
play.hint: Make the semicircle thinner until it breaks, then switch to the chain's arch. Put a load on it and slide it to and fro.
play.thickness_hint: From the inside of the arch to its outside; the span is 2 m.
play.load_hint: Measured against the arch's own weight.
play.at_hint: From the middle: −100 % at the left foot, 100 % at the right.
play.chain_hint: The hanging chain, upside down, through both feet and as high as the arch.
play.stands: The arch stands: the thrust line stays in the stone everywhere.
play.falls: The arch breaks: no thrust line stays in the stone everywhere. It opens at the red joints.

model.intro: A stone pushes, it does not pull. So an arch of loose stones stands as long as every joint is pressed together and the line along which the pressing runs – the thrust line – crosses every joint inside the stone.
model.chain: The hanging chain, upside down: it is pulled only along itself. An arch of this shape is pressed only along itself.
model.joint: Where the thrust line crosses joint j: the torque of all forces left of the joint about its middle, divided by the force across the joint. Both depend on the push at the foot, which the page seeks so that the line stays as near the middle as it can.
model.stands: The arch stands if some line crosses every joint inside the stone. The smallest λ for which such a line exists says how narrowly: 1/λ is the safety.

symbols.h: the arch's height above its feet
symbols.e: how far beside its middle the thrust line crosses the joint
symbols.m: the torque of all forces left of the joint about its middle
symbols.lambda: how far the line strays from the middle at most, as a share of half the thickness

sweet.chain: The best shape for an arch is a hanging chain, upside down – Robert Hooke noted it in 1675, and Antoni Gaudí designed with hanging chains. In the chain's arch the thrust line under its own weight stays in the middle of the stones, less than a hundredth of half the thickness off, however thick the stones.
sweet.semicircle: The semicircle does not have that shape. It stands only if its stones are at least 10.75 % as thick as its radius – 10.7 % with sixteen stones. At 10 cm on a metre it breaks; a pointed arch of the same span and thickness stands.
sweet.load: A load shifts the thrust line. Standing at the quarter point, it breaks the 25 cm semicircle at only 80 % of its own weight, the chain's arch of the same height not until 141 %.

computed.system: The arch is cut into stones of equal length, the joints across the centre line; each stone weighs as much as its quadrilateral and presses at its centroid. At every joint the pressing and the torque depend linearly on the push, the lift and the turning at the support; the page cuts from all possible values those that cross every joint inside the stone, and seeks the smallest λ by halving. The test finds for the semicircle the least thickness of 10.75 % of its radius that Milankovitch computed in 1907.
computed.left_out: Left out: the stones sliding (friction holds), their crushing (they are strong enough), the abutments giving way. The page shows where an arch breaks open, not how it falls.

at.plate: A square metal plate is fixed at its middle on a shaker, sand strewn on it. The shaker is driven by a slowly rising tone.
at.sand: At certain tones the plate rings loudly, and the sand runs together into lines and lies still there – a different pattern at each of these tones.

chladni.view: The plate from above with the sand on it

play.title: Choose the tone
play.hint: Choose one of the plate's tones, or sweep slowly with the slider. Between the tones the sand hardly jumps, and no pattern forms.
play.tones: The tones at which the plate rings
play.drive_hint: Logarithmic: every equal step is an equal musical interval.
play.sound_hint: The shaker's tone, loud when the plate rings, soft between.
play.swing_hint: How hard the plate's middle swings, measured against its swing at the lowest tone.

model.intro: A thin plate bends, and its stiffness resists. As with a string there are tones at which it keeps swinging by itself; to each belongs a shape with lines that stand still.
model.plate: The thin plate's equation: its bending stiffness balances its inertia. The edges are free.
model.tones: The tones: λ depends only on the shape; the plate's size and material set the pitch.
model.driven: Shaken at its middle, the plate answers with the sum of its shapes, each the more strongly the nearer its tone to the shaker's, and only if it moves at the middle.

symbols.w: how far the plate bends from rest
symbols.lambda: a shape's figure, the same for every square plate

sweet.still: The sand gathers where the plate does not swing at all: on the nodal lines. Everywhere else it is thrown up until it lands on one, and there it stays.
sweet.tones: A plate's tones are not overtones. A steel plate 24 cm square and 1 mm thick, shaken at its middle, rings at 102, 269 and 517 Hz – 2.62 and 5.05 times the lowest, not twice and three times as a string does.
sweet.middle: Shaken at its middle, the plate shows only the shapes that move there. Its lowest tone of all, at which it twists, has a node at the middle and stays silent.
sweet.history: Ernst Chladni showed the figures in 1787. Sophie Germain found the plate's equation and won the Paris Academy's prize for it in 1816; Gustav Kirchhoff put the free edges' conditions right in 1850.

computed.system: The deflection is written as a sum of products of Legendre polynomials up to degree 20; by Ritz, the shapes are those at which the energy stands still. The server finds their eigenvalues by Jacobi's rotations, once, and sends the shapes; the page sums them for every tone. The test holds the first values to Leissa's table (13.468 · 19.596 · 24.270 · 34.801 · 63.686). The sand is a drawing rule: grains are thrown up where the plate swings and slide to where it stands still.
computed.left_out: Left out: the shaker's hold at the middle (its mass and stiffness shift the tones a little), the plate's thickness beside its size, and how sand really jumps.
